title: BTC Looks Directionless After 7 Weeks of Losses
summary: In October we argued bitcoin's bear market ended in June. BTC has since lost its 50-week average and traded below the June low, an outcome that had never followed a comparable reclaim of the average. We withdraw our call and set out what may come next.
body_markdown:
*This report was originally sent directly to clients of Galaxy Trading and Galaxy Asset Management on Nov. 24, 2026. Trade or invest with Galaxy to receive the most timely research directly in your inbox.*


## Summary


Our Oct. 26 note, “[Why Now Is the Time to Add and Hold BTC](https://www.galaxy.com/insights/research/why-now-bitcoin-buy-hold-2026) ,” argued that bitcoin's bear market ended in June. Its technical argument is no longer valid.


After seven weekly closes above the 50-week average (traditionally viewed as the bear-market ceiling), bitcoin closed back below it in the week ended Nov. 8 and closed the following week below the 200-week average (historically the floor). On Nov. 20, BTC traded below its July 1 intraday low, reaching $55,100 on Nov. 21. Through the Nov. 22 close ($61,104), the June 30 closing low of $58,525 was intact by just 4.4%.


-


**Previously, no reclaim of this kind had been followed by a new low.** Since 2011, only two of the 13 prior reclaims of the 50-week average were followed by a daily close below the bear market low behind them. One was in 2021, the other in 2022, and they followed stays below the average of just one and 12 weeks, respectively. Not one of the five reclaims that ended longer stays was followed by a new low even intraday, nor was any of the seven that held for at least seven weeks. September's reclaim ended a 44-week stay, held for seven weeks, and has now been followed by a lower intraday low.


-


**But the signal had not been tested above a shallow low.** All five of those longer stays ended after declines of 76.7% to 92.7%, with the bear's final low already in. Only three prior reclaims followed shallower declines, all in 2021 and 2022, and two of them lost their lows. September's reclaim followed a comparatively mild 53% decline.


-


**Breaks of a standing low have led materially lower.** In the seven prior bear market cases in which bitcoin closed below a low that had stood for at least 60 days and from which it had rebounded at least 20%, the eventual low was at least 17% lower, with a median of 52%: about $48,500 and $28,200 if applied to the June low. One further case, in the mid-cycle decline of 2013, ended 2.8% lower.


-


**Late by the clock, early by the depth.** Nov. 22 was day 412 since the Oct. 6, 2025, record, compared to 163 to 406 days from high to low in the four prior bears, and day 946 since the halving, against 777 to 912 at the three prior lows. But the 53% decline to date compares with 77% to 93% in those bears; bitcoin has not closed a day below its realized price ($53,205), which every prior bear did for at least 140 days; and only two of the 13 bottom signals we track are met.


-


**The macro backdrop has deteriorated since June.** The two-year Treasury yield was 0.88 percentage point above the fed funds rate on Nov. 19, after a September rate increase. That gap is wider than at bitcoin's June low (0.51) but has narrowed from its Sept. 16 peak of 1.11; at the 2018 and 2022 lows it had peaked 82 and 148 days earlier and reached zero within 36 days after them. The S&P 500 was 1.5% below its record at the June low and closed 11.6% below it on Nov. 20, with the Nasdaq 100 19.8% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index 42.5% below theirs.


-


**Our view.** We withdraw our call that the bear market ended in June. We would treat a daily close below $58,525 as the start of a move to a materially lower low. The clock says this bear is overdue to end, the depth says it has further to fall, and we do not believe the price record alone can settle which.


We published our note on Oct. 26, three days before the Binance hack, eight days before the larger-than-expected Democratic sweep in the midterm elections and 17 days before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO. That was unfortunate timing, but we stand behind the analysis. In the note we said that a weekly close back below the 50-week average that was not regained within a month would invalidate its technical case, one of the four parts of the thesis. The cases for the other three (positioning, fundamentals and sentiment) are stronger now than when we published: third-quarter 13F filings showed advisors and wealth platforms adding to their bitcoin ETP holdings; the fundamental case for censorship-resistant, fixed-supply money remains potent; and sentiment about bitcoin ( *vis-à-vis* its sanitized cousin “blockchain”) is even worse. (Note that this report primarily focuses on the technical arguments from our Oct. 26 piece).


However, although bitcoin has until about Dec. 8 to regain the average, we must acknowledge that the bear market is very likely not over and that the reclaim is unlikely to come in time. Whether Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia on Nov. 23 can be the spark that pulls bitcoin back up to levels needed to end the bear market is unknown. This note examines the historical comparisons that do exist and the macro and positioning backdrop and sets out the paths ahead after a bruising stretch for risk assets.


## What we said, and what broke


The October note rested its technical case on one map. We wrote that the 200-week moving average is "the floor and the 50-week average the ceiling," and that in every completed bear market since 2011 "the first sustained run back above the ceiling came after the low." Bitcoin regained the 50-week average in the week ended Sept. 20, closing at $81,195 against an average of $78,787 and ending 44 straight weekly closes below it. The daily close peaked at $86,521 on Oct. 4, 47.8% above the June 30 closing low of $58,525 (Chart 1). Since then, however:


-


The week ended Nov. 8, BTC closed at $74,968, 0.7% below the 50-week average, after seven weekly closes above it.


-


The week ended Nov. 15, bitcoin closed at $65,189, 13.1% below the 50-week average and 4.1% below the 200-week average ($67,967).


-


The week ended Nov. 22, BTC closed at $61,104, 17.9% below the 50-week average and 10.4% below the 200-week average ($68,159).


-


That close was 24.7% below the Sept. 20 reclaim close and 51% below the record close of $124,824 on Oct. 6, 2025. The lowest daily close since the reclaim was $58,851 on Nov. 20, 27.5% below the reclaim close.


In October we noted that the four prior reclaims that ended stays of 20 weeks or more below the average never produced a weekly close more than 8.4% below the reclaim level. The week ended Nov. 22 closed 24.7% below September's. We also named a tripwire: a weekly close back below the 50-week average that was not regained within a month. That window will close around Dec. 8, and bitcoin would need to rise 21.8% from the Nov. 22 close to regain the average where it now stands ($74,401). We are not waiting for it.


Whether bitcoin has made a new bear market low depends on the basis. Intraday, it has: bitcoin traded at $57,661 on Nov. 20, below the $57,740 it touched on July 1, and as low as $55,100 on Nov. 21. On daily closes it had not through Nov. 22: the $61,104 close was 4.4% above the June 30 closing low of $58,525, and the lowest weekly close of the bear remains $59,517 (the week ended June 28). A daily close below $58,525 or a weekly close below $59,517 would confirm the break on the closing bases that the precedents in this note use.


**Chart 1:** *Bitcoin's daily close with its 50-week and 200-week averages, log scale. Rings mark each weekly close back above the 50-week average: green where the bear market low behind the reclaim held until the next record high, red where it was broken on a daily close before then, and orange for the Sept. 20, 2026, reclaim.*


## Has a 50-week reclaim ever been followed by a new bear market low?


Twice before, both in the 2021-22 bear market, and never after a reclaim like September's. This year's is so far a third on an intraday basis only.


A reclaim is a weekly close above the 50-week average after at least one weekly close below it. A new bear market low is a daily close below the lowest daily close since the record close then standing, made before the next record. The average begins in mid-2011, and of the 13 reclaims before September's, 11 were not followed by a new low. The two exceptions came in the same bear market (Table 1):


-


**Dec. 26, 2021.** Bitcoin had spent one week below the average and lost it again the following week. The low before the reclaim ($46,334 on Dec. 17, 2021) was 31% below the record close and nine days old, and it broke on Jan. 4, 2022.


-


**March 27, 2022.** Bitcoin had spent 12 weeks below the average and lost it again two weeks later. The low preceding the reclaim ($34,996 on Jan. 22, 2022) was 48% below the record close and 64 days old, and it broke on May 8, 2022.


Both ended at the same place: the Nov. 9, 2022, low, 66% and 55% below the lows that had broken.


**Table 1:** *Every Reclaim of the 50-Week Average Since 2011, and What Happened to the Bear Low Behind It. A reclaim is a weekly close above the 50-week average after at least one weekly close below it. The bear low is the lowest daily close since the record close then standing; its depth is measured from that record close. The last column of figures is the lowest daily close before the next record high (or through the as-of date) against that bear low.*


Two features set September's reclaim apart from the exceptions:


-


**The length of the stay below.** Five prior reclaims ended stays of more than 12 weeks (14, 20, 49, 49 and 62 weeks). Not one was followed by a new low on daily closes, weekly closes, or intraday. September's reclaim ended a 44-week stay.


-


**The time held above.** Seven prior reclaims held for at least seven weekly closes. Not one was followed by a new low. September's held for seven; the two exceptions held for one and two.


A third feature points the other way: the low preceding September's reclaim was shallow. All 10 prior reclaims that followed declines of 76.7% to 92.7% kept their lows, the five long stays among them. Only three followed shallower declines, all in 2021 and 2022, and two of them are the exceptions. The third, in July 2021, followed a 53.1% decline, the same as this year's to one decimal place. Its low held until bitcoin set a record in October 2021 and broke in May 2022, in the bear market that followed (Chart 2). The age of the low separates the cases less cleanly: the exceptions' lows were nine and 64 days old at the reclaim, the July 2021 low that held was five, and September's was 82.


**Chart 2:** *Each weekly close back above the 50-week average, by the age of the bear market low preceding it (horizontal) and the depth of that low below the record close (vertical). The size of each dot is proportional to the number of weekly closes below the average before the reclaim.*


Three cautions apply.


-


**The sample is small.** The 13 prior reclaims rest on only seven distinct bear market lows: six of them, in 2019 and 2020, sat above the same December 2018 low.


-


**The dividing lines are drawn after the fact.** The 12-week line is the longer of the two exceptions' stays and the seven-week line is September's own hold. The 44-week stay also turns on just $21: the week ended Sept. 6 closed that far below the average, and a close above it would have ended the stay at 42 weeks and left September's hold following a stay of one week.


-


**A reclaim made after a bear's final low keeps that low by definition.** That describes every long-stay reclaim before this year. Bitcoin had not regained the average after a long stay below it while the decline before it was still shallow, so September's was the first test of the signal in those conditions.


## What follows a break of a standing low


A standing low is a bear-to-date closing low that stood for at least 60 days and from which bitcoin rebounded at least 20%; a break is the first daily close below it. There are seven completed cases (three in 2014, two in 2018, and two in 2022) and one in this bear: on June 5 bitcoin closed below its Feb. 5 low of $63,495, and the June 30 low came 25 days later and 7.8% lower, so far the smallest extension on record (Chart 3, Table 2).


-


**All seven led materially lower.** The final low came 17.1% to 66.6% below the broken low, with a median of 51.8%. Late did not mean shallow: three of the four late breaks still ended 46% to 52% lower.


-


**Timing followed the age of the bear, and says nothing more.** The three breaks that came 113 to 181 days after the cycle high took 185 to 293 days to reach the final low. The four that came 302 to 378 days after it took 28 to 103 days. In each case the day of the break plus the days to the final low is the length of the bear, and those bears ran 364, 366 and 406 days, so the intervals cannot be projected onto a bear that is already older.


-


**Returns from the break were negative for six months.** Across all seven, the median return from the close on the day of the break was a loss of 9% after one month, 11% after three and 23% after six, and a gain of 25% after 12. Bitcoin was higher 12 months later after three of the four late breaks and one of the three early ones, which reflects the same arithmetic.


**Chart 3:** *Bitcoin's daily close after each break of a standing bear market low, against the broken low, by days since the first daily close below it. Solid lines are breaks that came 300 days or more after the cycle high and dashed lines are earlier breaks. Dots mark each bear's eventual lowest close.*


The June 30 low qualifies: it had stood for 145 days on Nov. 22, after a rebound of 47.8%. A daily close below $58,525 would come on day 413 of the bear or later: later than any prior break (the latest came on day 378) and after every prior bear had ended (by day 406). Applied to $58,525, the smallest prior extension points to about $48,500 and the median to about $28,200. The result holds under other thresholds (see Method and data).


One case is left out by definition. We count two record highs set within a year as one cycle, so the 71% decline between April and July 2013, which bitcoin had erased by November 2013, is not a bear market here. Its April 16, 2013, low stood for 80 days and broke on July 5, 2013, and the low came one day later, 2.8% lower. Counting it, seven of eight breaks led at least 17% lower.


## The clock: late


On three of the four calendar measures we track, this bear market is now older than any prior bear was at its low, and on the fourth it is about seven days past the latest of the last three (Charts 4 to 6).


-


**From the cycle high.** The four prior bears ran 163, 406, 364 and 366 days from the record close to the low. The June 30 low came on day 267; Nov. 22 was day 412.


-


**From the halving.** The three prior cycle lows came 777, 889 and 912 days after the halving. The June 30 low came on day 801; Nov. 22 was day 946.


-


**From low to low.** Prior cycle lows came 1,153, 1,431 and 1,425 days apart. This year’s June 30 low came 1,329 days after the Nov. 9, 2022, low; Nov. 22 was day 1,474.


-


**To the next halving.** The last three cycle lows came 513, 528 and 542 days before the next halving and the 2011 low 376 days before. The next one, at block 1,050,000, is about 506 days away (we estimate April 11, 2028): about seven days closer to it than the latest of the last three lows came, and inside the full range until about April 1, 2027. The June 30 low came about 651 days before the halving, earlier than any prior low.


The sample is thin, three or four cycles on each measure, and a four-year rhythm is an observation, not a law. It also gives no date for a later low. If the June low breaks, the bear will already be longer than any before it, and the only calendar window still open closes about April 2027, on the strength of the 2011 cycle alone.


**Chart 4:** *Bitcoin's daily close against the record close of each cycle, by days since that record close. Dots mark each bear's lowest daily close.*


**Chart 5:** *Days from the cycle high to the cycle low, from the halving to the cycle low, and from one cycle low to the next. For the current cycle the solid bar runs to the June 30, 2026, closing low and the hatched bar to Nov. 22, 2026.*


**Chart 6:** *Bitcoin's daily close as a multiple of its close on the day of each halving, by days since the halving, log scale. Triangles mark cycle highs and dots cycle lows; the shaded band spans the three prior lows.*


## The depth: early


By depth, the same bear market looks unfinished (Charts 7 to 10, Table 3).


-


**Drawdown.** The four prior bears fell 93%, 85%, 84% and 77% from the record close. Each was shallower than the last, but the largest step between them was eight percentage points. A bear that ended at the 53% decline of June 30 would be a step of 24 points.


-


**The 50-week average.** The deepest weekly close of this bear (week ended March 1) was 34% below the average. The four prior bears reached 55% to 60% below it.


-


**The 200-week average.** This bear has five weekly closes below it, the deepest by 10.4%. Counting from each cycle high to the next record high, the 2013-15 and 2017-18 cycles had five and one, by at most 1.4% and 2.8% and all after those cycles' lows; the 2021-22 cycle had 47, by as much as 32.4%. The week ended Nov. 22 closed 10.4% below the average, the deepest weekly close below it outside the 2021-22 cycle.


-


**Realized price.** Each prior bear closed below its realized price, the average cost basis of all coins, for 152, 304, 140 and 179 days. This one has not closed below it once: the realized price is $53,205, 12.9% below the Nov. 22 close. MVRV, the ratio of price to realized price, was 0.42, 0.56, 0.69, and 0.75 at the four prior lows, against 1.15 on Nov. 22.


-


**Capitulation.** The share of supply held at a loss reached 57% on Nov. 20, the highest of this bear and in line with the 55% to 61% at the four prior lows, and was 54% on Nov. 22. But realized losses over 30 days peaked at 3.6% of realized cap in February, against peaks of 7.3% to 16.7% in prior bears. Holders are underwater but have not sold at a loss on the scale seen in prior bears.


**Chart 7:** *Weekly closes against the 50-week and 200-week averages in each of the last four bear markets, by weeks since the cycle high, log scales. Shading marks weekly closes below the 50-week average, dots each bear's lowest daily close, and rings each reclaim of the 50-week average.*


**Chart 8:** *Bitcoin's weekly close against its 50-week average (top) and 200-week average (bottom), log scales. Red fill marks closes below the average and labels show the deepest in each bear. Shaded bands run from each cycle high to that bear's lowest daily close.*


**Table 3:** *Five Bear Markets Side by Side. Weekly closes below the 50-week average are counted from the cycle high through the week of the low. Days below realized price are daily closes between the cycle high and the next record high. MVRV, supply held at a loss, and the Fear & Greed Index are readings on the day of each low.*


**Chart 9:** *Bitcoin's daily close against realized price, the long-term holder cost basis, and CVDD (top, log scale) and MVRV (bottom). Shading marks daily closes below realized price; labels show each bear's lowest MVRV.*


**Chart 10:** *The share of bitcoin supply held at a loss and losses realized over 30 days as a share of realized cap (the market cap of the network’s coins based on the price when each coin last moved onchain). Labels show each series' maximum between a cycle high and 30 days after that bear's low (through Nov. 22, 2026, for this bear), not the reading on the day of the low.*


Table 4 sets out the levels. Four of them cluster between $48,400 and $53,200, 57% to 61% below the record close: realized price ($53,205), CVDD ($48,930), the smallest prior extension below a broken low ($48,504) and the long-term holder cost basis ($48,357). A low in that range would still be the shallowest on record, by 15 to 19 percentage points. The levels that would match prior bears sit lower, from the 200-week average at its deepest 2022 discount ($46,108) to a 77% drawdown ($29,123).


**Table 4:** *The Price Map. Levels on Nov. 22, 2026, from the nearest average above the close to the shallowest prior bear drawdown below it. The MVRV and long-term holder rows apply the ratios at the 2022 low, the least extreme of the prior bear lows, to the current value of each measure. The 200-week row applies that average's deepest weekly discount of 2022, the largest of any bear.*


## Holders and dormancy


The oldest coins are not the source of the selling; coins held for one to five years have been moving more (Charts 11 and 12).


-


The share of supply that has not moved in at least a year was 68.1% on Nov. 22, against 60.6% at the cycle high. About 2.9 points of that arrived on Nov. 22 alone: a large exchange moved its holdings to new addresses of its own on Nov. 22, 2025, which reset the age of about 580,000 BTC, and those coins passed the one-year mark together. The readings in between leave them out. Through Nov. 21 the share had risen 3.5 points from the June low, to 65.2%. The one-year share also rose between the high and the low in three of the four prior bears. The share unmoved for at least five years is 34.0%, up from 30.0% at the high.


-


Spending from coins unmoved for five years or more has slowed, to about 34,000 BTC a month in the 13 complete months from October 2025, from about 57,000 BTC a month in the 12 months before. One month, July 2025 (142,000 BTC), lifts the earlier average; the medians are about 32,000 and 40,000 BTC a month.


-


Long-term holder supply (coins unmoved for at least 155 days) has fallen 731,435 BTC from its July 26 peak, to 16.09 million BTC. In the 119 days since, 2.09 million BTC of such coins moved onchain: 46% had been held for 155 days to a year and 54% for longer, most of it (0.98 million BTC) for one to five years, about twice the 0.49 million BTC of such coins that moved in the 119 days before the peak. Supply unmoved for at least a year still rose 1,141,560 BTC because more coins aged past one year (2.27 million BTC, the large exchange's coins among them) than moved.


Rising dormancy is not evidence that a low is in: prior bears looked the same. It describes who is *not* selling, not whether the selling is over.


**Chart 11:** *Monthly BTC spent from coins that had not moved in at least five years, by the age of the coins when spent. The hatched bar is the month to Nov. 22, 2026. Horizontal lines show the monthly averages for the 12 complete months before the cycle high and the 13 complete months from it.*


**Chart 12:** *The share of bitcoin supply that has not moved in at least one, two, and five years. Circles on the one-year line mark each cycle high and low. The one-day step on Nov. 22, 2026, is a large exchange's coins passing one year after it moved them to new addresses of its own.*


## Macro, flows, and positioning


The backdrop has deteriorated since June: short rates have risen, stocks have fallen from their records, and ETP holdings have fallen since October (Charts 13 to 16).


### Rates


-


**Short rates are rising.** The two-year Treasury yield rose from 3.38% on Feb. 27 to 4.76% on Nov. 19, and the Federal Reserve raised rates in September: the effective fed funds rate went from 3.63% to 3.88% on Sept. 17. On Nov. 19 the two-year yield was 0.88 percentage point above the fed funds rate, a sign that the market is pricing a higher policy rate ahead. That gap was 0.51 percentage point at bitcoin's June 30 low and peaked at 1.11 percentage points on Sept. 16, its widest since November 2022; it has narrowed by 0.23 percentage point in the 64 days since.


-


**The two bears before this one ended as that gap closed.** At bitcoin's 2018 and 2022 lows the two-year yield was still 0.54 and 0.78 percentage point above the fed funds rate, but the gap had peaked 82 and 148 days earlier, at 0.90 and 2.62 percentage points, and it reached zero 19 and 36 days after the lows, when the market no longer priced a higher policy rate. The January 2015 low does not fit: the gap was 0.39 percentage point and did not reach zero until January 2019. This time the gap is wider than at the June low. It is also past a peak, as it was at those two lows: on Nov. 19 it was 0.23 percentage point below its Sept. 16 high, 64 days earlier, and still 0.88 percentage point above zero. Two cases are a thin record, and day to day the link is weak: the 90-session correlation between bitcoin's daily return and the daily change in the two-year yield is negative 0.02.


**Chart 13:** *Bitcoin's daily close with the two-year Treasury yield and the effective fed funds rate (top), and the two-year yield minus the fed funds rate (bottom). Dashed vertical lines mark bitcoin's lowest daily close in each bear.*


### Stocks and semiconductors


-


**Semiconductors.** The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index set a record close of 14,635 on June 22, eight days before bitcoin's June 30 low, and closed at 8,409 on Nov. 20, 42.5% below it. In the six weeks to Nov. 20 the index fell 33.1% and bitcoin 28.7%. Over the whole bear the two have diverged: since bitcoin's Oct. 6, 2025, record close the index is up 24.1% and bitcoin is down 52.9%. The correlation of their daily returns is 0.61 over the last 30 sessions and 0.43 over the last 90.


-


**Stocks.** At bitcoin's June 30 low the S&P 500 was 1.5% below its record close and the VIX was 16.5. On Nov. 20 the S&P 500 closed 11.6% below its Oct. 6 record and the Nasdaq 100 19.8% below its own.


-


**Precedent.** The S&P 500 fell at least 20% in only one of the three bitcoin bears before this one. Between bitcoin's cycle high and its low, the S&P 500's largest decline was 7.4% in 2013-15, 11.3% in 2017-18, and 25.4% in 2021-22 and the Nasdaq 100's was 8.2%, 14.8% and 35.5%, respectively. By contrast, bitcoin fell 77% to 85% during these periods. In 2018 and 2022 the S&P 500's own low for the decline came within a month of bitcoin's. In this bear the S&P 500's largest decline was 9.1% through bitcoin's June low and is 11.6% through Nov. 20; the Nasdaq 100's was 12.1% and is 19.8%.


-


**Correlation.** Bitcoin is trading more closely with other assets than usual: the 90-session correlation of its daily returns with the Nasdaq 100's is 0.52, higher than on 87% of sessions since 2014, and with gold's 0.51, higher than on 99%.


-


**Volatility.** The VIX closed at 35.9 on Nov. 20, its first close at or above 35 since April 2025. Of the nine earlier such episodes since 2011, the six that began outside a bitcoin bear were followed by a median 12-month gain in bitcoin of 142%, with one loss. The three that began during one (August 2011, February 2018 and March 2022) were followed over 12 months by a 41% gain, a 50% loss and a 42% loss; by definition they came before their bears' lows, which were 73%, 53% and 59% lower. Which group this episode joins depends on whether the June low holds.


-


**Liquidity.** Liquidity measures are mixed and have been a weak guide to bitcoin: the combined assets of the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, and the Bank of Japan were $17.19 trillion on Nov. 13, 5.9% less than a year earlier in dollars (3.2% less at constant exchange rates), U.S. net liquidity was 3.9% higher and M2 was 5.6% higher in September, and since 2011 the year-over-year changes in the first two have had weekly correlations of 0.14 and 0.26 with bitcoin's.


**Chart 15:** *Bitcoin, the S&P 500, the Nasdaq 100 and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index in each bitcoin bear since 2013: the change from bitcoin's cycle high to the end of each span (top) and each series' largest decline from its own highest close within the span (bottom).*


### Flows and positioning


-


**ETPs.** U.S. spot bitcoin ETPs hold an estimated 1.24 million BTC, 9.7% below the Oct. 9, 2025, peak of 1.37 million BTC. They added 84,729 BTC ($6.65 billion) between the June 30 low and the Oct. 4 high and have shed 71,339 BTC ($4.95 billion) since, with outflows on 22 of 35 sessions. Holdings remain 1.5% above the July 13 trough of 1.22 million BTC, which we named in October as a second tripwire.


-


**13F filings.** According to[third-quarter 13F filings](https://www.galaxy.com/insights/research/bitcoin-etp-13f-institutional-holdings-q3-2026-wealth-channel-wells-fargo) , including late filings through Nov. 20, advisors and wealth platforms (registered investment advisors, wealth managers, wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms) held a record 144,972 BTC-equivalent of U.S. spot bitcoin ETPs at Sept. 30, and their 40.6% share of all 13F-reported holdings was also a record (Chart 17). Their holdings have risen for nine straight quarters since the only decline, in the second quarter of 2024. Their net buying in the third quarter, 25,496 BTC-equivalent, was the largest since the funds launched in January 2024. Three banks accounted for nearly all of it, and as we wrote on Nov. 19, one bank's increase sat almost entirely at its dealer and trading units, which we read as dealer positioning rather than demand from wealth clients.


-


**Derivatives.** Positioning is not stressed. Perpetual futures funding averaged 4.3% annualized over the seven days to Nov. 22 and has not been negative on that basis in the last 30 days; it reached minus 24.5% on Nov. 15, 2022, six days after that bear's low. Leveraged funds were net short 6,771 BTC of CME futures on Nov. 17, against 26,055 BTC four weeks earlier.


**Chart 16:** *Estimated BTC held by U.S. spot bitcoin ETPs (left axis) and bitcoin's daily close (right axis).*


**Chart 17:** *BTC-equivalent held in U.S. spot bitcoin ETPs by Form 13F filers at each quarter end, stacked by type of holder, with advisors and wealth platforms at the bottom. Filings through Nov. 20.*


## Sentiment and the bottom scorecard


Sentiment, like the share of supply held at a loss, has already reached levels seen at prior lows on a daily reading (Chart 18).


-


Our proprietary Bitcoin Fear & Greed Index fell to 5.2 on Nov. 21, the lowest of this bear and its lowest reading since June 30, 2022 (4.8); only 0.5% of daily readings since the start of 2011 have been lower. It read 6.2 on Nov. 22, and 5.7, 2.9, 6.2 and 6.4 on the day of the four prior lows.


-


Duration is the difference. The index has spent six days at or below 10 in this bear, against 57, 12, 24 and 32 days in the four prior ones (counted through 30 days after each low), and its 30-day average is 32. Around the last three lows, that average bottomed at 11.7, 8.5 and 17.2, in each case after the low (by 23, three and 28 days).

The thresholds are set in-sample, at about the least extreme of each signal's lowest readings within about a month of the 2015, 2018 and 2022 lows, so all 13 were met within 180 days of each of those lows by construction. On the exact day of each low, 11, nine and four were met. The count of four understates the 2022 low: four more signals (MVRV, net unrealized profit/loss, reserve risk and the drawdown) missed by about 1% or less, because their thresholds are that day's own readings, rounded. On Nov. 22 two were: price below the 200-week average, and more than 12 months since the cycle high. Not one of the four onchain valuation signals (MVRV, MVRV Z-score, net unrealized profit/loss and reserve risk) has been met at any point in this bear.

## What comes next


The record gives two readings of the same market, and they disagree on time and price.


-


**If the clock prevails,** this is the last stretch of an old bear: it is already older than any before it on three of four measures, and the fourth window closes about April 2027. The nearest cluster of support is $48,400 to $53,200, which would make this the shallowest bear on record and the first without a sustained period below realized price.


-


**If the depth prevails,** the bear converges on the valuations at which prior bears ended: levels between $29,100 and $46,100 and a sustained period below realized price. The record gives no date for that path: after the two 2021-22 exceptions the low took a further 185 and 309 days, in a bear that still ended on day 366, and this one is on day 412.


### Where we come out


-


We withdraw the October call that the bear market ended in June. The signal it rested on has failed.


-


A daily close below $58,525 would be a break of a standing low, and all seven prior bear market breaks led to a close at least 17% lower. We would not treat such a close as a buying signal by itself.


-


The evidence that this bear is late is real but rests on three or four cycles. The evidence that it is shallow is broad: the drawdown, both moving averages, realized price, MVRV, realized losses and the 11 of 13 bottom signals not met. We do not believe the price record alone can settle which prevails.


-


This note revisits only the technical argument of the October report.


### What would change our view


-


**Toward the low being in:** a weekly close back above the 200-week average (now $68,159) and then the 50-week average (now $74,401), with the June weekly closing low ($59,517) holding on weekly closes.


-


**Toward a deeper bear:** a weekly close below realized price ($53,205), because every prior bear that closed below it spent at least 140 days there; or ETP holdings falling through the July 13 trough of 1.22 million BTC.


-


**A caution on capitulation readings.** We track four: realized losses over 30 days above about 7% of realized cap, negative perpetual funding, a 30-day Fear & Greed average below 17 and a two-year Treasury yield at or below the fed funds rate. No capitulation reading reliably marked a prior low on the day. Realized losses peaked 132 to 380 days before the last three lows and were above 7% on the day of only one; the two-year yield was above the fed funds rate at all three; and the 30-day Fear & Greed average was below 17 at only one. Funding, on record only since July 2022, was positive on a seven-day average on the day of the 2022 low and negative the next day. Three of the four have already occurred in this bear. The fourth has not: realized losses over 30 days peaked at 3.6% of realized cap, against 7.3% to 16.7% in prior bears.


We are not trying to call the low. The calendar says this bear is older than any before it; the depth says it has not yet done what every prior bear did, closing below realized price and forcing holders to sell at a loss. Until one gives way, we will judge the market on weekly closes rather than headlines. We are watching three things: whether the June lows hold on a closing basis ($58,525 on a daily close and $59,517 on a weekly one), whether advisors and wealth platforms keep adding to their bitcoin ETP holdings, and whether the two-year Treasury yield falls back toward the fed funds rate. A weekly close back above the 200-week average, then the 50-week average, would bring us back toward our October view. A break of the June lows would tell us the depth is winning.


## Definitions and Methodologies


Prices are daily closes at 00:00 UTC.


A *weekly close* is the daily close of a week ending Sunday, and the 50-week and *200-week averages* are simple averages of completed weekly closes.


A *reclaim* is a weekly close above the 50-week average after at least one weekly close below it.


A *bear market low* is the lowest daily close since the record close then standing, and a *new low* is a daily close below it. On these closes the 2021-22 bear's low is Nov. 9, 2022 ($15,758); the Nov. 21, 2022 close was $20 higher; and a series that dates the low to that day moves that bear's day counts by 12 days. A *cycle high* is a record daily close later followed by a close at most half of it; two such highs within a year count as one cycle, dated to the later one. Section 2 instead measures each low from the record close standing at the time of the reclaim, so Table 1 counts the reclaim of July 2021, which came before that cycle's November 2021 high.


A *standing low* is a bear-to-date closing low that had stood for at least 60 days when it broke and from which a daily close had risen at least 20% in between. With 30 days and 20%, there are 10 breaks, and nine ended more than 10% lower (the smallest extension was 5.1%); with 60 days and 25%, all seven ended at least 17.1% lower; with 90 days and 25%, all four at least 45.6%; and with 45 days and 30%, all seven at least 45.6%. Days since the halving count the halving day as day zero; the October note counted it as day one. Intraday lows are used only where stated.


*Realized price* is the average cost basis of all coins, each valued at the price when it last moved onchain; *realized cap* is that value summed across all coins, and *MVRV* is price divided by realized price. *Long-term holders* are coins that have not moved in at least 155 days. Coins are aged from their last onchain movement, so a transfer between an owner's own addresses counts as a movement and resets a coin's age; the amounts of coins that moved, by age, include such transfers.


*CVDD* (cumulative value-days destroyed) is a floor model built from the age and price of coins as they are spent. Supply held at a loss is the share of coins that last moved at a price above the close. *ETP holdings* are our estimate, built from the holdings of the converted trusts and daily dollar flows converted at the same day's close.


*13F holdings* are the bitcoin behind the ETP shares that Form 13F filers report at each quarter end, with holder types assigned per filing manager from its name, its Form ADV client mix and review of the largest filers; net buying is the change in shares held at the quarter's bitcoin per share, not the change in value.


*Perpetual funding* is an open-interest-weighted average across perpetual futures markets, annualized and averaged over seven days, with history from July 28, 2022.


*CME positioning* is from the CFTC's Traders in Financial Futures report and is expressed in BTC. The Fear & Greed Index is Galaxy’s proprietary composite of momentum, volatility, valuation, profit-taking and flow inputs on a scale of 0 to 100, with its history recomputed under the current method.


The *two-year Treasury* yield is the constant-maturity series and the *fed funds rate* is the effective rate, both daily; the gap between them is measured in percentage points.


*Stock figures* are daily closes of the S&P 500, the Nasdaq 100 and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, measured on the dates given or the last exchange session before them.


*Correlations* are of daily log returns on common exchange sessions, with bitcoin's return measured from one session's 00:00 UTC close to the next, and each percentile compares the latest 90-session value with every session since the start of 2014.


A *VIX episode* is the index's first close at or above 35 after more than 90 days without one, counted from 2011; it began during a bitcoin bear if it fell between a cycle high and that bear's lowest daily close, so such an episode came before its bear's low by definition, and the latest one cannot be classed until it is known whether the June low holds.


*Central bank assets* are the total assets of the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan, converted to dollars at each day's exchange rates (the Bank of Japan's are monthly, through October 2026). U.S. net liquidity is the Federal Reserve's total assets less the Treasury's cash balance at the Federal Reserve and overnight reverse repurchase agreements. Year-over-year changes compare with 365 days earlier, or 12 months for M2.
